content.value_statement: Graph projects need clear methods for building and analyzing relationships. This skill guides NetworkX workflows for algorithms, formats, and visual outputs.
actual_capabilities: Explains how to create directed, undirected, and multigraph structures.
Guides common algorithms such as shortest paths, centrality, clustering, and communities.
Covers graph generators for random, lattice, tree, and social network models.
Documents graph import and export formats including edge lists, GraphML, JSON, CSV, and SQLite.
Provides visualization guidance for static, interactive, and publication-ready network figures.
limitations: It depends on the user environment having Python and needed libraries installed.
Very large graphs may exceed memory or runtime limits in local sessions.
It does not verify data quality before analysis unless the user requests checks.
It provides guidance and examples, not a managed graph database service.

use_cases.title: Map Relationship Data
use_cases.description: Turn edge lists or tables into NetworkX graphs and inspect their structure.

use_cases.title: Measure Network Influence
use_cases.description: Compute centrality, paths, clustering, and communities for social or citation networks.

use_cases.title: Prototype Network Models
use_cases.description: Generate synthetic graphs and compare their structure with real network data.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Basic Graph
prompt_templates.prompt: Use NetworkX to model these entities and relationships. Explain the graph type, nodes, edges, and key checks.

prompt_templates.title: Analyze Network Metrics
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze my network with NetworkX. Recommend centrality, clustering, connectivity, and community methods for this dataset.

prompt_templates.title: Choose Import and Export Formats
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me choose NetworkX file formats for this graph workflow. Compare readability, attributes, size, and tool compatibility.

prompt_templates.title: Design a Full Network Study
prompt_templates.prompt: Plan a NetworkX analysis from raw relationship data through validation, algorithms, visualization, and reproducible outputs.

output: Recommended graph type based on relationship direction and repeated interactions.
Suggested metrics for influence, bridges, communities, and disconnected groups.
A visualization plan that uses layout, color, and labels to highlight structure.

output_examples.input: Pick a format for saving a weighted graph with node attributes.
output_examples.output: GraphML is recommended when attributes matter and other tools need to read the graph. CSV is better for simple edge tables.

output_examples.input: Compare a real network to synthetic small-world and scale-free models.
output: A workflow for generating comparable model graphs with fixed random seeds.
Metrics to compare degree distribution, clustering, path length, and components.
A reporting structure for explaining which model best matches the observed network.

best_practices: Choose the graph type before loading data, especially for direction and parallel edges.
Set random seeds for graph generators and force-directed layouts.
Validate node identifiers, edge weights, and connected components before interpreting metrics.
anti_patterns: Do not use dense matrices for large sparse graphs unless memory is acceptable.
Do not compare centrality scores across different graph types without context.
Do not rely on a visualization alone when quantitative checks are required.

faq.question: What is NetworkX best for?
faq.answer: It is best for Python graph modeling, network analysis, algorithms, import and export, and exploratory visualization.

faq.question: Can this skill handle directed graphs?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers directed graphs, undirected graphs, multigraphs, and directed multigraphs.

faq.question: Does it support graph visualization?
faq.answer: Yes. It explains static drawing, layout selection, styling, interactive options, and publication-ready figures.

faq.question: Can I use it with CSV or pandas data?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes guidance for pandas edge lists, CSV files, matrices, JSON, GraphML, GML, and SQLite examples.

faq.question: Is it suitable for very large graphs?
faq.answer: It can guide large graph work, but memory and runtime limits depend on the local environment and algorithm choice.

faq.question: Does it run analysis automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides guidance and examples that an AI assistant or user can adapt to their own environment.
